title: Charging Quantum Batteries with Chiral Squeezing
authors: Borhan Ahmadi, André H. A. Malavazi, Janine Splettstoesser, Paweł Horodecki, Lei Du
abstract: We propose a quantum-battery charger based on a driven bosonic Kitaev chain (BKC), where chiral squeezing converts passive input fluctuations into ordered, non-passive battery states. While a coherent input pulse exhibits phase-sensitive chiral transport, the charging dynamics is dominated by bidirectionally propagating fluctuations that are amplified and squeezed into orthogonal quadratures at opposite chain ends. In contrast to conventional phase-preserving amplifiers, our scheme stores largely extractable energy and achieves a work-like signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) near unity, even in the presence of thermal noise and moderate symmetry-preserving disorder.
summary: The paper proposes using a driven bosonic Kitaev chain as an advanced charger for quantum batteries. By exploiting chiral transport mechanisms, the system converts passive input fluctuations into highly ordered, extractable energy. This results in a high work-like Signal-to-Noise Ratio that remains robust even when thermal noise or moderate disorder is present.
main_problem: The research addresses how to efficiently charge quantum batteries by converting unavoidable input fluctuations into ordered, extractable work using a driven bosonic Kitaev chain.
main_result: The proposed scheme achieves a near-unity work-like Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) robustly against thermal noise and moderate disorder. This is achieved because fluctuation dynamics dominate the stored energy over coherent input contributions.
method: The analysis uses quantum Langevin equations in quadrature representation to track first moments and covariance matrices, allowing for the calculation of stored energy and ergotropy.
model_or_system: The system is a driven bosonic Kitaev chain (BKC) coupled to two harmonic oscillator batteries at its ends. The dynamics are governed by a total Hamiltonian incorporating hopping ($h$), parametric pumping ($\Delta$), coupling, and external driving/dissipation.
key_observables: Work-like Signal-to-Noise Ratio ($	ext{SNR}_{	ext{work}}$), Charging Efficiency ($\eta$), Stored Energy ($E_\alpha$), and Quadrature Fluctuations ($\delta x^2, \delta p^2$).
important_parameters: Chiral squeezing parameter $r$, disorder strength ($\delta\omega$), chain half-length ($N$), and thermal occupancy ($n_{th}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on linear Gaussian descriptions of the dynamics, assuming a stable regime where $|h| > |\Delta|$ to avoid parametric instability.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate charging dynamics comparing coherent vs. fluctuation energy contributions and showing $	ext{SNR}_{	ext{work}}$ dependence on chain length and disorder strength.
paper_structure: The paper develops the model using Hamiltonian/Langevin equations, analyzes the role of chiral transport in converting fluctuations to stored energy, quantifies performance metrics like SNR and efficiency, and finally tests robustness against various types of disorder.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed theoretical framework for engineering quantum energy storage, moving beyond simple coherent pumping by harnessing inherent quantum noise via engineered lattice dynamics (chiral squeezing).

figures.caption: FIG. 1: (a) A bosonic Kitaev chain (BKC) with nearest- neighbor hopping h and parametric pairing ∆, which is equivalent to two decoupled Hatano-Nelson chains for the x and p quadratures with opposite chiralities. (b) Schematic of the chiral charger: a driven-dissipative BKC of length 2N + 1, with local losses κj and chiral squeezing weights e±r, is excited at the central site j = 0 by a short coherent pulse. The two end sites (j = ±N) are coupled to the batteries through coupling g.

FIG. 2: Charging dynamics. (a) Coherent contribu- tions to the left- and right-battery stored energies, Ecoh L and Ecoh R . (b) Quadrature-resolved fluctuation contribu- tions to the left-battery stored energy, EL,δx2 and EL,δp2. (c) Same as (b) for the right battery, ER,δx2 and ER,δp2. (d) Extractability of the stored energy, quantified by WL(t)/EL(t) and WR(t)/ER(t). (e, f) Overall charging efficiency η, with the chain kept on for all times in (e) and switched off at t = t⋆in (f). The vertical dotted lines indicate the switch-off time t = t⋆. Parameters: N = 5, ∆/h = 11/12, g/h = 5/12, κj/h = 8.3 × 10−4

FIG. 3: Work-like signal-to-noise ratio SNRwork(t⋆), eval- uated at t = t⋆, as a function of the chain half-length N for several thermal occupancies nth. Inset: representa- tive signal-to-noise ratio SNRwork con (t) for a conventional phase-preserving amplifier with uniform on-site gain (see Note 4 of the SM [70]). All other parameters are the same as in Fig. 2.

FIG. 4: SNRwork(t⋆) versus static hopping disorder (left) and pump disorder (right), for a fixed chain half-length N = 5. For each disorder strength, 50 random realiza- tions are sampled. The green solid curves with error bars show the mean ± standard deviation, the blue dashed curves denote the median, and the shaded regions indi- cate the 16th–84th percentile range. All other parame- ters are the same as in Fig. 2.

FIG. 5: Ergotropy W(t⋆) as a function of the battery- energy fluctuation σE(t⋆), evaluated at the optimal charging time t⋆. Each curve is obtained by varying the chain half-length N from 2 to 6 at fixed bath thermal occupancy nth, as in Fig. 3. The data lie almost on the same straight line, showing that W(t⋆) and σE(t⋆) grow in a correlated manner as N increases. All other param- eters are the same as in Fig. 2.
